hints: Focus on the class of each alcohol, primary, secondary or tertiary, because that controls what oxidation can do.
Recall that a primary alcohol can stop at an aldehyde or go on to a carboxylic acid, while a secondary alcohol stops at a ketone.
Look for the alcohol that can be oxidised, but cannot be oxidised twice to give two different products.
walkthrough:
**Classify each alcohol**

Think about how many alkyl groups are attached to the carbon bearing the OH. That tells you the class and the oxidation behaviour.

$\text{primary} \rightarrow \text{aldehyde} \rightarrow \text{carboxylic acid}$, $\text{secondary} \rightarrow \text{ketone only}$, $\text{tertiary} \rightarrow \text{no reaction}$

**Count the possible products**

A primary alcohol gives two possible products under warming with excess oxidant. A secondary alcohol gives just one ketone. A tertiary alcohol gives none.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$$

**Apply to the four alcohols**

Butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are primary, so two products. 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary, so zero products. Butan-2-ol is secondary, so exactly one product, butanone.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$$

options.A: Butan-1-ol is a primary alcohol. It oxidises first to butanal and then to butanoic acid, so two possible oxidation products, not one.
options.B: Butan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol. It oxidises to one ketone only, butanone, which resists further oxidation. This is exactly one possible product.
options.C: 2-methylpropan-1-ol is a primary alcohol. It oxidises to 2-methylpropanal and then to 2-methylpropanoic acid, so two possible products.
options.D: 2-methylpropan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol with no hydrogen on the C-OH carbon. It is not oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI), so it gives zero products, not one.
